Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Frog: First Encounter with the Poem

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the title and asks children what they know about frogs — where they live, what they eat, what sound they make. Responses are gathered aloud and celebrated briefly.
Teacher reads the entire poem aloud with clear expression, pausing at vivid images — the darting tongue, the webbed feet, the hiding in leaves. Children follow in their textbooks (pp.55–56).
Teacher reads the poem a second time, inviting children to read along softly. Attention is drawn to the bouncy rhyming couplets and how the rhythm echoes the frog's hopping movement.
Teacher leads a brief whole-class sharing: which image surprised you most — the frog hiding in leaves, the darting tongue, or the proud croak? Children respond in one or two words or a short phrase.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's rhyming couplets give it a naturally musical lilt; modelling an expressive read-aloud at a brisk, bouncy pace helps children feel that rhythm before they analyse it. The first-person voice — the frog speaking as 'I' — is central to the poem's tone and worth pointing out gently so children engage with the speaker's pride and playfulness.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.56): four short-answer questions on the frog's life in the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recites the opening stanza aloud and invites children to join in. The frog's dual home — ponds and drains — is recalled quickly as a shared starting point for the questions ahead.

Let us Think — A. (p.56): Teacher asks each of the four questions one at a time, giving children a moment to find the answer in their textbooks before sharing aloud. Questions cover where the frog sits, how it catches food, how it moves, and what helps it hide.

For each question, one or two children share their answer aloud. Teacher echoes and extends: for example, after 'the tongue darts out', teacher points to the poem's exact lines and asks the class to read them together softly.

Whole-class close: teacher asks one open question not in the task — 'The frog says it feels proud in its pond. What do you think makes it proud?' — and takes two or three brief responses before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often answer comprehension questions with single words; gently prompting 'Can you say that in a full sentence?' after each response builds the habit without slowing the discussion. All four answers are directly available in the poem text — steer children back to the page if they guess rather than read.

periods.activity_title: Talk Like a Frog: Discussion and Tongue Twisters

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.56): four guided discussion prompts comparing frog and human experiences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the first discussion prompt: 'What would it feel like to live like a frog — in water and on land?' Children turn to a partner and share for a couple of minutes, then two pairs report to the class.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.56): Teacher guides prompts two, three, and four in sequence — imagining high hops, contrasting frog and fish lives, and comparing webbed feet to scuba flippers. Each prompt gets a pair-share and brief whole-class report.

Let us Speak — A. (p.58): Teacher introduces the tongue twisters and models the first one slowly, then faster. Children practise each of the three tongue twisters in pairs, gradually increasing speed. Pairs challenge each other to a count of correct repetitions.
Three volunteers each perform one tongue twister for the class at speed. Teacher closes by noting the 'fr' and 'fl' sound clusters that make these twisters tricky and fun.

periods.teacher_notes: The discussion prompts work best when children are encouraged to use the poem's own language — 'webbed feet', 'damp', 'croak' — in their answers, which reinforces vocabulary alongside oracy. The tongue twisters all begin with 'fr' or 'fl' clusters; let children notice this themselves rather than announcing it.

periods.activity_title: Listen, Repeat, Draw: Sound Pairs and Frog's World

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen — B. (p.56): teacher reads vowel-sound word pairs aloud; children listen and repeat.
Let us Listen — My Frog's World (p.60): teacher reads instructions aloud; children draw and annotate their frog's habitat.

time_bands.activity: Let us Listen — B. (p.56): Teacher says each word pair clearly — 'bet–bat', 'set–sat', 'men–man', 'leg–lag', 'met–mat' — at normal speed, then repeats each pair. Children listen the first time, then echo both words of each pair together on the second round.

Teacher repeats selected pairs ('men–man', 'leg–lag') and asks: 'What is the one sound that changes?' Children identify the vowel shift by ear. This is not a writing exercise — the focus stays on the ear and the voice.

Let us Listen — My Frog's World (p.60): Teacher reads the four instructions aloud slowly and clearly. Children draw a setting for their frog, add the frog, write two or three words from the poem around the drawing, and colour it in their notebooks or on the textbook page provided.
Two or three children hold up their drawings and say one word they wrote and why they chose it. Teacher affirms all contributions and closes the activity.

periods.teacher_notes: The vowel-pair listening task focuses on short-e versus short-a sounds — a common confusion at this stage — so unhurried, clear pronunciation of each pair matters more than speed. For 'My Frog's World', children who finish the drawing quickly can add a short sentence of their own about the frog; those who need more time can skip colouring and focus on the words.

periods.activity_title: Joining Words: Conjunctions in the Frog's World

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.57): fill-in-the-blank task using conjunctions and, but, because, or in context.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the four conjunctions — 'and', 'but', 'because', 'or' — on the board and elicits from children what each one does: 'and' adds, 'but' contrasts, 'because' gives a reason, 'or' offers a choice. Examples are drawn from the poem: 'I live on land and water too.'

Let us Learn — A. (p.57): Teacher reads each sentence aloud with a pause at the blank. Children think individually, then share with a partner. The class agrees on the answer together, and teacher confirms — drawing attention to the meaning-clue in each sentence that signals the right joining word.

Teacher writes two new sentence frames on the board — one needing 'because' and one needing 'but' — taken from the poem's themes (e.g. 'The frog hides in leaves ___ its colours match the plants'). Children complete them orally, then one child per frame writes the answer on the board.

Quick round: teacher calls out a conjunction and a child makes up a sentence using it. Three or four children take a turn. Teacher closes by noting that conjunctions help join ideas, just as the poem joins images of land and water into one creature's story.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently confuse 'because' and 'so' — both signal cause — so it helps to ask 'Does this sentence explain why, or does it say what happened next?' when a child is stuck. All fill-in answers are verifiable from the poem's own language, so returning to the poem page is always a valid move.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.57–58): rearrange scrambled animal-action words into correctly ordered sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes one scrambled set on the board — 'hunts/night/the/silently/tiger/at' — and models the process of finding the subject first, then the verb, then the remaining words. The class builds the correct sentence together.

Let us Learn — B. (pp.57–58): Children work through the remaining four scrambled sets in pairs, writing the correctly ordered sentence for each. Teacher circulates, prompting with 'Who is doing the action?' and 'What is the action word?' to help pairs who are stuck.

Pairs share answers aloud in sequence. For each sentence, the class votes 'agree' or 'suggest a change' with a thumbs signal. Disagreements are resolved by reading the sentence aloud and checking whether it sounds natural and complete.

Teacher connects the activity to the poem: 'The frog hops, swims, hides, croaks — these are all action words, and the sentence puts them in the right place.' A child volunteers to say one poem line that has a clear subject and action.

periods.teacher_notes: The scrambled sentences all feature animals and their movements, which links naturally to the poem's imagery of the frog as an active creature. Children who finish early can write one scrambled sentence of their own — using any animal — and swap with a partner to solve.
materials: Notebooks or scrap paper for pair work

periods.activity_title: Write Back to Hopper: A Friendly Reply

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.59): write a short friendly letter in reply to Hopper the frog's message, share with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Hopper's letter aloud expressively (textbook p.59), pausing to note its friendly greeting, the details about Hopper's life — lily pad, water puddles, croaking, eating mosquitoes — and the closing question 'What do you like to do?' Children listen for what Hopper tells us about itself.

Teacher models a reply on the board, thinking aloud: 'Dear Hopper, / Hello! My name is… / I like to… / I also enjoy… / Your friend, …' The class suggests two or three ideas for the middle sentences and teacher writes them, showing how a reply picks up details from the original letter.

Children write their own reply letters in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, prompting those who are stuck with 'What is one thing you really like to do?' and helping with spellings on request. The letter should have a greeting, two or three sentences about themselves, and a friendly close.

Three or four children read their letters aloud to the class. After each reading, classmates share one thing they liked hearing. Teacher affirms details that mirror Hopper's voice — responding to the mosquito question, mentioning water or rain, etc.
Teacher closes by noting that letters are a real form of communication — people write to say hello, share news, and ask questions — just as Hopper did from the lily pad.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often want to write very long letters at this stage; gently nudging them toward two or three focused sentences keeps the task manageable and the sharing quick. Hopper's letter models the informal letter format neatly — greeting, body, close — so keeping the textbook open for reference during drafting is helpful.

periods.activity_title: Find the Frogs and Draw a Duck

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p.62): find five hidden frogs in the nature-scene picture.
Let us Do — B. (p.63): follow the five-step diagram to draw a duck in the space provided.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the activity with a brief link to the poem's image of the frog hiding in leaves and grass — 'My colours match the plants and trees.' Children are told they will find five frogs camouflaged in a picture.

Let us Do — A. (p.62): Children look at the nature-scene picture and circle or mark each hidden frog they find. After individual searching, children compare findings with a neighbour. Class counts together how many were found.
Teacher briefly connects the camouflage puzzle to the poem's theme: hiding well is one of the frog's real survival skills, not just a fun detail.

Let us Do — B. (p.63): Teacher talks through each of the five steps in the duck-drawing diagram on the textbook page, demonstrating the shape at each stage in the air or on the board. Children follow the steps in the textbook space provided, adding their own details at the end.
Children hold up their duck drawings briefly. Teacher asks one child: 'What would your duck and the poem's frog have in common?' — eliciting 'water', 'swimming', 'webbed feet' or similar.

periods.teacher_notes: The hidden-frog picture directly embodies the poem's camouflage stanza, so connecting the two is natural and worth a brief mention rather than a long explanation. For the duck-drawing, some children will complete quickly and can add a background setting; those who find the steps tricky benefit from the teacher drawing step one and two on the board as a guide.

periods.activity_title: Puzzle, Explore, and Celebrate: Closing the Chapter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — C. (p.64): move three crayons to change the direction of the fish-shape puzzle.
Let us Explore (p.64): choose two water creatures and share a few facts about them with the class.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do — C. (p.64): Teacher shows the fish-shape diagram and explains the challenge: move exactly three crayons so the fish faces the opposite direction. Children work with physical crayons at their desks or trace on paper, trying different moves. After an unhurried attempt, teacher guides the class to the solution step by step.

Brief whole-class share on the puzzle: 'Did anyone find a different way?' Teacher connects the lateral-thinking nature of the puzzle to curiosity about water animals — the theme that runs through the chapter.

Let us Explore (p.64): Children who have had time to look up facts choose two water creatures from the list — puffer fish, jellyfish, seahorse, starfish, octopus, catfish — and share two or three facts aloud with the class. Children who have not prepared choose one creature and say one thing they already know or can guess from its name.

Teacher closes the chapter by leading a final choral recitation of the last stanza of the poem — 'With webbed feet, I swim with ease, / And leap so high in joyful breeze!' — inviting children to say it with as much frog-pride as they can.

periods.teacher_notes: The crayon puzzle is a spatial-reasoning challenge; resist giving the solution too quickly — an unhurried attempt where children try and discard moves builds persistence. The 'Let us Explore' sharing works even when children have not researched in advance, because naming what they already know about a seahorse or octopus is a valid and productive contribution.
materials: Crayons or sticks for the fish puzzle

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 55 beginning "I flick my tongue to catch my food." Which of the following correctly describes how the frog catches its food?

options.label: A
options.text: It waits quietly near a pond and snaps its jaws shut.

options.label: B
options.text: It flicks out its tongue very quickly to catch food.

options.label: C
options.text: It uses its webbed feet to scoop insects from the water.

options.label: D
options.text: It chases insects across the grass until it catches them.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student is thinking of a crocodile's hunting style rather than the frog's tongue action in the poem.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a confusion between the frog's feeding method and its swimming adaptation described elsewhere in the poem.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student has not connected the speed of the tongue flick to catching food, imagining a chase instead.

items.item_stem: In the poem, the frog says its colours help it hide. Where does it hide, and what two things does it hide among? Write your answer in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The frog hides in the grass and among leaves because its colours match the plants and trees around it.

items.item_stem:
Your teacher will say two words. Listen carefully and decide whether the two words sound the same or different. Choose the correct answer for each pair.
1. "leg" and "lag"
2. "met" and "met"
3. "set" and "sat"

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Different (short-e versus short-a). 2. Same. 3. Different (short-e versus short-a).

items.item_stem: Think about how a frog's life is different from a fish's life. Tell your class two differences between them, using what you know from the poem about the frog. Speak in complete sentences.

expected_elements: Names one way frog lives on land and water.
Names one way fish lives only in water.
Speaks in at least two complete sentences.

items.item_stem: Hopper the frog wrote that its favourite hobby is sitting in water puddles and croaking. Write one sentence as the opening of your reply letter that addresses Hopper by name and mentions something from its letter.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any sentence that greets Hopper by name and refers to something from Hopper's letter, such as sitting in puddles, croaking, or eating mosquitoes — e.g. 'Dear Hopper, I loved hearing about your favourite hobby of sitting in water puddles!'

items.item_stem: Write a short reply letter to Hopper the frog. In your letter, include a greeting, two or three sentences about something you enjoy doing, and a friendly closing. Use what Hopper shared about its own life to make your reply feel like a real conversation.

expected_elements: Letter has a greeting and a friendly close.
Includes two or more personal details about self.
Responds to or acknowledges something Hopper said.

Choose the correct conjunction from the box to complete each sentence.

[ and · but · because · or ]

1. The frog leaps high, ___ it must watch out for snakes.
2. Frogs can live in ponds ___ on land.
3. The frog hides well ___ its colours match the leaves.

| Seahorse | Has eight arms |
| Octopus | The male carries the babies |
| Starfish | Can grow back a lost arm |
| Jellyfish | Has no bones and can sting |
